ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the upper branch of the figure there is a resistor R, and the node at the right end of the resistor is connected downward through an inductor L to the lower common wire; the input voltage u1 is marked on the left side, indicating that it is applied across the entire R-L series branch; the output voltage u2 is marked on the right side, indicating that it is taken across both ends of the inductor L. Then reason: The inductor impedance is jωL, therefore the voltage division relationship is U2/U1 = jωL/(R + jωL). Its phase is arg(U2/U1) = 90° - arctan(ωL/R). It is required that u2 leads u1 by 60°, so 90° - arctan(ωL/R) = 60°, that is, arctan(ωL/R) = 30°. Therefore ωL/R = tan 30° = 1/√3. Substituting R = 100 Ω and ω = 1000 rad/s gives L = R tan30° / ω = 100 × 0.57735 / 1000 = 0.0577 H = 57.7 mH.

Image description first: The attached circuit diagram shows a resistor labeled R in the upper series path. To the right of the resistor, a vertical inductor labeled L connects down to the lower conductor. The input voltage u1 is marked on the left side across the whole R-L series branch, and the output voltage u2 is marked on the right side across the inductor. Both voltage reference arrows are drawn downward.

Reasoning: Choose the series branch current I as the phasor reference. Then the resistor voltage is U_R = IR, in phase with I, so draw it horizontally. The inductor voltage is U_L = IωL, leading I by 90°, so draw it vertically upward. The input voltage is the phasor sum U1 = U_R + U_L, the diagonal of the right triangle, while the output voltage is u2 = U_L. Since u2 must lead u1 by 60°, and U_L is at 90° relative to the current reference, U1 must be at 30° above U_R. Therefore tan 30° = U_L / U_R = (IωL)/(IR) = ωL/R. Solving gives L = R tan 30° / ω = 100 × 0.57735 / 1000 = 0.057735 H = 57.7 mH.
